chapter_theme: The god Sudanjanan continues to set out for Civakan the road ahead, hermitages, rivers, forests, hunters and wondrous pools, giving the route as a map of landmarks and closing with a prophecy of the king of the middle country, a marriage and the friends' return.

cast.role: the god, once the dying dog Civakan helped, who carries him out of prison and here describes his road
the hero, addressed by the god as காளை, மொய்ம்ப and other epithets
the king of the middle country who will receive Civakan, foretold in 1214-1215
Civakan's companions, foretold to rejoin him

1191.reading: Beside the mountain river there are plantains with ripe clustered fruit, mango trees with sweet honeyed fruit, and jackfruit trees that have borne their thorny, nectar-filled fruit.
1191.nuance: The god's route speech to Civakan, begun in the previous run, continues here; the abundance is a traveller's assurance of food on the way as much as praise of the place.

1192.reading: Gold, long gems of bright lustre and land a yojana wide shine there: this is the cool Chitrakuta that the ascetics, never wearied, long for.
1192.nuance: சித்திர கூடம் names a hill of hermitages; the verse sets the ascetics' desire on a place rather than on wealth, though the place is itself described as shining with gold and gems.

1193.reading: The great river Anjana comes down roaring like drums and great cascades, dragging bamboo, sandalwood and diamonds and carrying away heaps of gems.

1194.reading: The god points out the hermitage, the snowy mountain, the river of clear sand and the grove ringed by surapunnai trees that brush the moon, and bids Civakan hold to his way without slackening his pace.
1194.nuance: The deictic இது ... அது ('this is ... that is') makes the speech a map shown from above, fitting a god who has carried the hero through the sky.

1195.reading: In the hermitage of the great ascetics who mortify themselves, the jasmine with sharp buds climbing the kurundu tree has the beauty of gold-like women clasping the side of the husbands they are joined to.
1195.nuance: The image of the faithful wife embracing her husband is set inside the hermitage of those who have renounced: the poem keeps the householder's ideal and the ascetic's place side by side without comment.

1196.reading: The wide land of the konrai and kura forest, where bees and honey-bees play the yazh to the songs of those who reap the millet with sickles, stretches twelve kaathams.

1197.reading: Beyond that boundary Civakan will see the beauty of a land of fitting renown, with strong toddy, gold pots filled with flowers, and fields ringed by the sweet sound of drums.
1197.nuance: சீர்த்தக்க நாட்டு may name the Takka land, where the patikam (20) places Civakan's later marriage to a merchant's daughter, or simply mean 'a land of fitting excellence'; the division of the words does not settle it.

1198.reading: In the lovely land Civakan crosses, ripe areca fruit split from their spathes and tear the honey-heavy joints of the tall sugarcane, and the vaalai fish lick the drip and fight with the varaal.
1198.nuance: Like the patikam's opening landscape of Emangadam (31), fruit falling on fruit is the stock sign of a rich land; the vocative காளை marks this as speech to the hero.

1199.reading: On the way past that land a river will appear, covered with bunches of champak flowers, scented by the hair of the women of the land, with bees swarming down its whole length.
1199.nuance: யங்கநாட் may be read அங்க நாட்டு, the Anga land, or as அங்கு அந் நாட்டு, 'of that land there'; the route's geography turns on it.

1200.reading: That river, the god says, sweeps up many bright gems and, sharing its own excellence to feed the world, is a courtesan with a gold-girdled waist; if Civakan swims across it quickly,
1200.nuance: The courtesan here is a figure of open-handed bounty: she shares her நலம் with the whole world as the river shares its gems. The sentence does not end in this verse; it runs into 1201.

1201.reading: a forest will appear, ringed by the huts of the forest people, built of white elephant tusks, thatched with the white hair of the yak, and crammed with honey, meat, roots, unripe and ripe fruit.
1201.nuance: The hunters' huts are rich in what the forest gives, meat among them, which prepares the harsher judgment on the forest people in 1205.

1202.reading: Everywhere the sounds mingle and swell: the harsh drum, the voice of those churning toddy, the call of the long-trunked elephant, the long voice of the gem-bearing falls, and the cry of the frightened deer mixed with the roar of the killing tiger.

1203.reading: The god tells Civakan that there are four pools, set with fine gems, as hard to see as the virgin daughters of a gold-wheeled emperor, which will show themselves to him.
1203.nuance: The comparison with a cakravartin's secluded daughters makes the pools a guarded treasure that appears only to one who is worthy, a promise to the hero more than a description.

1204.reading: Of the pools, one is filled with red petals, one has a quickening water that turns dark iron to gold, one cures all diseases together, and one, beyond nectar or other than it, is a pool of opening blue water-lilies.
1204.nuance: இரத நீர் is rasa-water, the alchemist's transmuting fluid; the verse lists it beside a healing water without remark. The count of four in 1203 does not fit the items cleanly: அமிர்தம் அல்லது ஒன்று may name a nectar pool and leave the lily pool as a fourth, or describe the lily pool as other than nectar.

1205.reading: The forest dwellers with killing bows in hand, men of wretched bodies and forms of sin itself, show themselves suddenly, destroy travellers, and take their bodies, thinking escape impossible for them.

claims.claim: those who live by killing travellers are sin embodied

1205.nuance: The judgment பாவ மூர்த்தியர், 'embodiments of sin', falls on the forest people as a class; the god names it as a danger of the road, not as a teaching, and the closing words (உய்வகை அரிதென) may be either the victims' plight or the killers' reasoning.

1206.reading: If Civakan passes, with no thought for it, the pool on which men's eyes fasten as women's eyes fasten on a noble man, keeping it on his left, the bowmen will at once bow and gaze at him.
1206.nuance: The instruction works like a charm: a ritual way of passing the pool turns the killers of 1205 into worshippers. What makes them bow is not said.

1207.reading: Beyond, for five kaathams, the way runs sweetly, like the swaying grace of a dancing woman whose anklet-bells ring and whose girdle flashes as the bees play the yazh in her garland.

1208.reading: The straight red road, they say, lies on flower-pollen, strewn with fresh blossoms as if a garland had fallen, with jasmine and kaththigai, and is like the minds of chaste women.
1208.nuance: The chaste woman's mind is the measure of a road that has no forks: karpu is figured as singleness of direction. Compare 1212, where women's hearts are the figure for a road that divides.

1209.reading: The god bids Civakan see, as he goes, the great springs like jewelled bowls and, between them, the cool groves like flower baskets adorned with long gem-like blossoms.

1210.reading: On the right, like the moon, will appear Vanagiri, ringed by groves where falls cast down like nets roar, firmer than the chastity of high-born women with jewelled breasts and girdles of gold.
1210.nuance: As in 1208, the chastity of women is the poem's standard of firmness, here for a mountain; the qualifier குலத்தலை மகளிர் ties that firmness to women of good family.

1211.reading: They say it is a mountain where songs of love arose and wander, because those who live there keep without wavering the holy word of the Great One whose red feet the Dark One bowed his sacred crown upon.

claims.claim: the Dark One (Krishna or Vishnu) bowed his crown at the feet of the Great One whose word the mountain's dwellers keep

1211.nuance: கரியவன் 'the dark one' bowing to பெரியவன் 'the great one' is most naturally Krishna (or Vishnu) bowing to a Jina, a Jain ranking of gods; the verse does not name either. மரியவர் and மதன கீதம் are hard: the dwellers may be ascetics or celestials, and the link between their keeping the word and the songs of love is not clear.

1212.reading: After he has passed the jewelled hill hard to climb, the road splits into many forks, like the hearts of women on the path of marriage that may not be changed, and the god says he will tell the true straight way so that Civakan may know it.
1212.nuance: The phrase மாற்றரு மணநெறி மகளிர் is doubtful: if it means married women, the verse contradicts 1208's straight road like chaste women's minds; it may instead mean women of an unchanging scent-path, a garland figure.

1213.reading: There is a spring ringed with blue lilies where bees swarm; beside it a round slab of gem-stone; there a vengai tree where bees hum with longing; and beside the vengai a red road has been laid out.
1213.nuance: The chain of landmarks, each placed by the last (அச்சுனை மருங்கில், வேங்கையின் மருங்கில்), is the poem's way of making a route memorable.

1214.reading: The god tells Civakan that when he has crossed the whole forest scented with kanthal like open hands, he will meet the king of the middle country with his bright spear and garland, and that this meeting is his good fortune.
1214.event: Sudanjanan tells Civakan that after the kanthal forest he will meet the king of the middle country.
1214.nuance: குணம் அது, 'that is the good', sets the meeting as a fortune to be met rather than a deed; the god foretells what the patikam (21) summarizes as the king coming out to receive the hero.

1215.reading: The god says that while Civakan lives there, after the king who guards the earth has given him his flawless daughter, all his friends, drooping like stars that have lost the white moon, will come to him there.
1215.event: Sudanjanan foretells Civakan's marriage to the middle country king's daughter and his friends' coming to him.
1215.nuance: The prophecy names the marriage and the friends' reunion that the patikam (22-23) gives as events; the image of stars bereft of the moon, which the patikam gives to the younger brother, is here given to the friends.

links.note: The patikam tells how the king of the middle country (மத்திம தேய மன்னன்) came out to receive Civakan on seeing his bow; in 1214 the god foretells that meeting (மத்திம தேயம் ஆளும் ... கண்ணுறு குணம்) before the journey begins.
links.teaches: The meeting the summary reports as the king's response to the hero's bow is, in the god's speech, a fortune already laid out on the road, so the poem frames a political welcome as the fruit of a divine guide's foreknowledge.

links.note: The patikam compares Civakan's younger brother, desolate, to a star that has lost the moon (மதியம் கெடுத்த வய மீன்); 1215 gives the same image (வெண்மதி யிழந்த மீன்போல்) to all his friends.
links.teaches: The stars-without-the-moon figure belongs to the hero's whole circle rather than to one kinsman, so Civakan is the moon to every follower and his absence dims them all alike, brother and friends.

links.note: The patikam says the lion-like royals of the middle country kept Civakan and gave him a girl in marriage; 1215 has the god foretell that the king will give him his daughter while he stays there.
links.teaches: Read with the patikam, the marriage that looks like the royals' choice to bind a strong stranger was promised in advance by the god, so the hero's marriages come to him as foretold gifts rather than conquests.

links.note: Kural 916 scorns women who spread a base goodness (புன்னலம் பாரிப்பார்) to all; in 1200 the river, sharing its own goodness to feed the world (தன்னுடைய நலம் பகிர்ந்து உலகம் ஊட்டலின்), is called a courtesan with approval.
links.teaches: The same act, a நலம் given to everyone, is a mark of baseness in the Kural and of bounty in the epic's simile, which shows that the Kural's contempt lies in the sale of a person and not in the sharing itself.

gains.a: a reminder that the courtesan figure carried moral weight, so the epic's praise of the river is a deliberate reversal and not a neutral image
gains.b: a case where the courtesan's openness is turned to praise once nothing personal is sold, sharpening what exactly the couplet condemns

links.note: Kural 974 says greatness exists only for one who holds himself as single-minded women (ஒருமை மகளிர்) do; 1208 likens a straight unforking road to the minds of chaste women (கற்புடை மாதரார் மனம்).
links.teaches: Both texts use the chaste woman's mind as the model of an undivided line, for a man's greatness in one and for a road in the other, showing that karpu was read as singleness of direction rather than as purity alone.

gains.a: a precedent that the chaste mind is a figure of oneness, which explains why the epic chooses it for a road without forks
gains.b: a concrete picture, a straight road strewn with flowers, of what the couplet's single-mindedness looks like in space

links.note: Kural 329 says those whose work is killing are base in the eyes of the discerning; 1205 calls the forest bowmen who kill travellers embodiments of sin (பாவ மூர்த்தியர்).
links.teaches: The couplet judges a deed, killing, while the epic fixes the same judgment on a forest people as a class, so the pair shows how the ethics of not-killing could harden into a picture of hunters as sin incarnate.

gains.a: the couplet's ground for the label: the hunters are condemned for the work of killing, not for being foresters
gains.b: evidence of how the principle was applied to whole groups living by the bow, which the couplet's general wording does not show

links.note: 1208 likens the straight red road to the minds of chaste women; 1212 likens a road splitting into many forks to the hearts of women on the path of marriage.
links.teaches: If மணநெறி மகளிர் are married women, the same speech makes women's minds the figure of both the one straight road and the forking one, showing the simile serves the road and carries no settled view of women.

source_issues: Verse 1205 line 1 கையடு is flagged as possibly கையொடு with a lost vowel sign; both readings (bows that kill in hand, or bows in hand) give sense, and it is left as printed.
Verse 1200 ends mid-sentence (நீந்தினால) and its clause completes in 1201.
Verse 1204 lists the pools in a way that does not cleanly yield the four of 1203; the division around அமிர்த மல்லதொன் is doubtful.
Verse 1211 line 3 மரியவர் and மதன கீதம் do not construe clearly; the line may be corrupt.
Verse 1212 line 2 மாற்றரு மணநெறி மகளிர் is ambiguous (married women, or a scent figure).
